verdict.reasoning: Patient states onset was “about a week ago,” describes “a weird swelling on my elbow… It’s not painful at all… it’s slightly warm, and I kind of feel like it’s a bit fluid inside,” and confirms it is the left elbow.
When asked about injury, patient replies: “No, not really. Not that I know of. I haven't noticed anything,” indicating no trauma to the left elbow.
Doctor asks, “And has this happened before?” Patient answers, “No, no, I haven't noticed that before. I don't have any, like, history of… seeing this,” indicating no prior similar episodes.

Patient says, “I think I have something like osteoarthritis…,” and later confirms diagnosis: Doctor: “Has anyone ever told you that?...” Patient: “Yes, a few years ago.” Doctor clarifies it was a GP: “Was that a GP…?” Patient: “A gp.”
Doctor asks, “are you on any medication on a regular basis?” Patient replies, “No, no,” confirming no regular medications.
Doctor advises, “I would take ibuprofen regularly… That's 400 milligrams, three times a day. And you should take that after food,” which is a plan to start ibuprofen 400 mg TID after food.
Patient states, “I'm allergic to… to peanuts. That's pretty much all I had to say about my medical history,” confirming peanut allergy.
Doctor asks, “Are you allergic to any medication?” Patient responds, “No, not that I know of,” indicating no drug allergies.
Work: Doctor asks if job is physical; patient says, “Not really, no. I just, you know, sit at the desk.” Activity: Patient says, “I do do some sports. I run regularly. Like two, three times a week.”

Patient has a personal rheumatologic condition: osteoarthritis diagnosed by a GP. The fact states “no personal… history of rheumatologic diseases,” which contradicts this. Family history is uncertain: “in my family, I'm not sure,” not a clear negative.

Location: Doctor confirms “Left elbow. Okay.” Warmth: Doctor asks, “Is it hot compared to the surrounding skin?” Patient: “It's a bit warm?” Doctor: “Yes, it's a bit warmer.” Swelling is the presenting issue observed via video exam.

Tenderness: Doctor asks about pressing; patient replies, “On the tip of the elbow? It's okay. Just like next to it, like where the swelling is? It's a bit…” indicating adjacent tenderness. Dry skin: Doctor notes, “I noticed the skin was a bit dry on the tip of the elbow.”

While not phrased as a formal finding, doctor states, “your joint doesn't look like… septic arthritis,” and discusses that concern would be if it became “very red, very painful.” This implies absence of erythema and severe tenderness at present.

Doctor says, “This seems like what we call the bursitis… an inflammation of one of the fluid sacs around the joint.” This is in the context of painless swelling with mild warmth and fluid sensation described by patient and seen on exam.

Osteoarthritis is a pre-existing diagnosis: patient: “Yes, a few years ago” when asked if a doctor confirmed it. There is no indication of acute change, so recording it as a stable known condition is consistent with transcript.
Doctor instructs, “I would take ibuprofen regularly… That's 400 milligrams, three times a day. And you should take that after food, not an empty stomach. If you get any heartburn, stop taking it.”

Doctor outlines bloods: “check for inflammatory markers, infection, rheumatological antibodies… and also check for things like gout as well,” matching inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatologic antibodies, and gout panel.

Doctor says, “we're going to arrange some blood test forms to be sent out to your house and there'll be instructions within that pack about where to go to get those blood tests done,” matching sending forms with instructions.

Doctor advises, “if the elbow was to become very red, very painful, and the redness was to spread or become more intense, then you need to get on the phone or have a video appointment… as soon as possible,” which is urgent reassessment advice.

Doctor: “we can arrange a follow up appointment… where we can have a look at your joint… Actually… doesn't have to be face to face. If it's more convenient… over the phone… over video… That's your call. But you contact us after you've had the blood test done, and we can review things then,” matching follow-up options after results.

Same as plan-004: Doctor instructs urgent contact “if the elbow was to become very red, very painful, and the redness was to spread or become more intense,” constituting criteria for urgent reassessment.
Same as plan-005: Doctor plans follow-up “after you've had the blood test done” and notes it can be “face to face… over the phone… over video,” confirming follow-up modality options after results.
